text: Experiment zero four: A fuse in a circuit. In this experiment, we will understand how an electrical fuse protects a circuit.
The components required are: a three-volt battery ePod, a red LED ePod, three jump wires, and a pencil lead between zero point five and one millimeter.
Here is the circuit diagram from the workbook. The pencil lead is inserted into the positive circuit path between the battery and the red LED.
Connect battery negative to LED negative. Then connect battery positive to one side of the pencil lead, and the other side of the pencil lead to LED positive.
With the pencil lead intact, the red LED glows! The graphite pencil lead acts as an electrical conductor and completes the circuit path.
Now, let us simulate what happens when a fuse blows by gently breaking the pencil lead.
The pencil lead snaps, separating into two pieces! The red LED immediately turns off. Breaking the lead creates an open circuit, stopping all electrical current.
In real electrical systems, a fuse contains a thin filament that melts when current increases excessively. By melting, it breaks the circuit and protects expensive appliances from damage.
In tinkering: you can explore replacing the pencil lead with a single-strand wire to observe continuity restored.
